push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette:
Henryk is a 76-year-old widowed man of Polish descent who works part-time as a cashier at a grocery store in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a visit to his primary care physician, during which he broke down describing nightmares that had persisted for over two years. His PCL-5 score of 67 places him in the severe range, and what emerged across the intake sessions was a clinical picture shaped profoundly by his experience as a civilian caught in an active conflict zone during a visit to relatives in Eastern Europe.

Henryk had traveled abroad to see aging cousins he had not visited in decades. Within days of his arrival, the region came under sustained bombardment. He described sheltering in a basement for nearly three weeks, listening to the percussion of artillery, watching through a narrow ground-level window as vehicles burned in the street outside. It was the vehicles that seemed to concentrate the horror most acutely - a truck engulfed in flame, the smell of fuel and something worse, the sight of people running and then not running. When he finally reached safety and flew home, he told himself he was fine. He was not fine.

The memories that returned to him were almost entirely visual - flashes of orange light against a dark ceiling, the silhouette of a burning vehicle, a face contorted in a scream he could not hear through the glass. When these images came, Henryk did not simply remember; he relived. The basement returned to him fully, and he would find himself gripping the edge of his register at the grocery store, certain for a moment that the fluorescent hum above him was something else entirely. These intrusions, arriving without warning during his shifts, reinforced what he had already begun to believe: that the world he had returned to was not the safe world he had once inhabited. He had come to feel that danger was ambient, structural, woven into ordinary life in ways he had simply failed to notice before. The memories did not feel like the past. They felt like evidence.

At other times, the same events came back to him stripped of all feeling - a flat, dissociated recall, as though it had happened to a stranger he had read about in a newspaper. This emotional numbness offered no real relief; if anything, it deepened his conviction that something in him had been permanently altered, that he was no longer capable of being the man he had been - the one who drove his late wife to her appointments, who fixed things around the house, who moved through the world with a certain quiet competence. That man, he believed, had not come home from Eastern Europe.

His hypervigilance had become the organizing principle of his waking life. At the register, he watched customers carefully - tracking hands, reading faces, noting anyone who lingered too long near the entrance. He had difficulty falling asleep most nights because some part of him remained convinced that relaxing his guard would be the mistake that cost him everything. This sustained state of alertness fed back into the intrusions: a customer's raised voice, the backfire of a delivery truck in the parking lot, the particular quality of late-afternoon light through the store's plate glass - any of these could pull the visual memories forward with sudden force, and the reliving would begin again. The threat monitoring and the memories had become mutually sustaining in a way Henryk could not have articulated but clearly felt as a trap.

In response, he had stopped driving entirely - even as a passenger, the sight of other vehicles produced a constriction in his chest he could not manage. He had begun pushing away any moments of pleasure or warmth, finding them dangerous in a way he struggled to explain, as though allowing himself to feel safe would lower a guard he could not afford to lower. These strategies kept him contracted and isolated, and the contraction itself seemed to confirm his worst appraisals: that people could not be trusted, that faith - in others, in God, in the basic order of things - had been revealed as naive. The avoidance left him with fewer experiences to contradict the memories, and the memories continued to instruct him that the world was exactly as dangerous as he now believed it to be.

What finally brought Henryk in was a conversation with his youngest daughter, who had driven two hours to see him and found him sitting in the dark. He had not been able to tell her what was wrong. What he most hoped for, he said quietly at the end of the first session, was to be able to drive again - to feel, just once, like himself.
